content: The certainty of the evidence supporting most critical outcomes was rated as very low. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued 14 recommendations regarding drug treatment for non-severe hypertension during pregnancy. Dissemination and implementation of these recommendations should involve all stakeholders and organizations providing care to pregnant women at international, national, and local levels. It is essential to improve access to and strengthen the capacity of healthcare facilities to deliver high-quality services to all women during childbirth. The acceptability of drug treatment for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy may vary among women, depending on their understanding of the risks associated with hypertension during pregnancy, the cost of medications, and potential side effects. There is insufficient data on how much women value health outcomes associated with different classes of antihypertensive drugs, and there is no direct evidence on the cost-effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, or impact on health equity of these treatments. The GDG noted that while antihypertensive drugs may provide health benefits for pregnant women with non-severe hypertension, these women require regular outpatient monitoring and review by antenatal care providers. The GDG also acknowledged that alpha-agonists (e.g., methyldopa) and beta-blockers are reasonable options for antihypertensive treatment. Clinicians should select a drug regimen tailored to the woman’s individual clinical situation, considering factors such as pre-existing antihypertensive treatment, side effect profiles, risks (including potential fetal effects), cost, local availability, and the woman’s preferences. Methyldopa is considered the safest option, is included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, and is widely available in many countries. Evidence suggests that calcium channel blockers should be avoided. Trials have used various oral beta-blockers (e.g., acebutolol, atenolol, labetalol, metoprolol, propranolol) at different doses, making it difficult to determine the optimal beta-blocker or dosing regimen for this indication. Atenolol and metoprolol are listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines and are widely available. The use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and sodium nitroprusside should be avoided due to safety concerns. The WHO plans to disseminate these recommendations through its regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. The recommendations will also be available on the WHO website and in the WHO Reproductive Health Library. Updated recommendations will be shared during scientific conferences and meetings attended by relevant WHO staff. The document will be translated into six UN languages and distributed through WHO regional offices. Technical assistance will be provided to regional offices interested in translating the recommendations. Successful implementation of these recommendations into national programs and healthcare services requires well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes for adaptation and implementation. This may involve developing or revising national guidelines or protocols. The recommendations should be adapted into locally appropriate documents to meet the specific needs of each country and healthcare service, with any changes made transparently. Healthcare providers should receive training and supportive supervision on prescribing antihypertensive drugs safely and counseling women on the risks and benefits of available options. In settings where new antihypertensive drugs are introduced or recommended practices are changed, additional training and monitoring may be required. Antenatal appointments may be scheduled every two to four weeks if hypertension is well-controlled, and more frequently if it is poorly controlled. Local and international professional societies play a crucial role in this process, and an inclusive and participatory approach should be encouraged. Healthcare providers should discuss risks, benefits, and treatment options with women to facilitate informed decision-making. The GDG identified several knowledge gaps that need to be addressed through further research, including understanding the outcomes valued by women and their families regarding antihypertensive drug options, identifying the most effective antihypertensive drug for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy (including effects on the fetus and newborn), and optimizing the management of non-severe hypertension during pregnancy at primary care and community levels, particularly in low-resource settings. Updating training curricula and providing training will enhance impact and facilitate implementation. Standardizing care by incorporating these recommendations into existing maternity care packages and protocols can encourage behavior change among healthcare providers. Monitoring and evaluating guideline implementation should be part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. This can involve clinical audits or reviews to monitor indicators such as the proportion of women with non-severe hypertension receiving antihypertensive therapy and the proportion progressing to severe disease or experiencing adverse outcomes. Monitoring should align with WHO standards for improving maternal and newborn care quality, including the availability of medicines, supplies, and equipment for managing hypertension during pregnancy. The recommendations will be reviewed annually by the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) to prioritize new and existing questions for development and updating. If new evidence emerges that could impact the current evidence base, the recommendations may be updated. If no new information is identified, the recommendations may be revalidated. Following publication and dissemination, any concerns about their validity will be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, and plans will be made to update the recommendations. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to include in future updates.
